title: Days and months — a week that's really a counter
goal: Name days, months, and dates — and discover that Slovenian day names aren't names at all but frozen ordinal numbers, with Wednesday meaning "middle".
bekal: name the seven days and twelve months, plus the forms *v ponedeljek* / *v sredo*
give dates with the Genitive: *petnajstega marca*
use the ordinals *prvi, drugi, tretji* for dates, floors, and queue numbers

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Izpit je v petek
dialogs.intro: Eva and Budi are sitting in the university cafeteria. Budi is copying the timetable into his phone and discovers that Slovenian day names hide some arithmetic.

lines.speaker: Eva:
lines.id: Because we have an exam on Friday.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: V petek? Mislil sem, da je v četrtek.
lines.id: On Friday? I thought it was on Thursday.
lines.literal: on Friday? thought I-am, that is on Thursday.

lines.speaker: Eva:
lines.text: Ne, četrtek je prost. Petek, petnajstega.
lines.id: No, Thursday is free. Friday the fifteenth.
lines.literal: no, Thursday is free. Friday, of-fifteenth.

lines.speaker: Eva:
lines.text: Ja. In torek je drugi dan, četrtek četrti.
lines.id: Yes. And torek is the second day, četrtek the fourth.
lines.literal: yes. and Tuesday is second day, Thursday fourth.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: So the week is really a counter.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Vse se ujema. Ob kateri uri je izpit?
lines.id: It all fits. What time is the exam?
lines.literal: all self fits. at which hour-loc is exam?

lines.speaker: Eva:
lines.id: At ten in the morning. Don't be late!

notes: **Slovenian day names are ordinal numbers.** *Torek* comes from *drugi* (second), *četrtek* from *četrti* (fourth), *petek* from *peti* (fifth). The prettiest is *sreda* — from *sredina*, middle — because in the old count the week started on Monday, so Wednesday sits exactly in the middle. German does the same with *Mittwoch*.

**Ponedeljek = po nedelji**, "after Sunday". And *nedelja* itself means "the day without work" — from *ne delati*, not to work. So the whole Slovenian week reads like one sentence: no-work day, the day after no-work day, the second, the middle, the fourth, the fifth, and then *sobota* — the only one from outside, via Hebrew *shabbat*.

**V ponedeljek, but v sredo.** To say "on (a day)", use *v* with the **object** form — not the place form. The masculine days don't change (*v ponedeljek, v torek, v četrtek, v petek*), but *sreda*, *sobota*, and *nedelja* are feminine, so their ending becomes *-o*: **v sredo, v soboto, v nedeljo**.

**Dates use the Genitive.** *Petnajstega* = "on the fifteenth". The month follows suit: *petnajstega marca* (March 15), *prvega maja* (May 1). If you're just stating today's date without "on", the form is ordinary: *Danes je petnajsti marec.*

**Mislil sem** and **Ne zamudi!** are two sneak previews. The first is the past tense — notice the *-l* ending, said **MEES-leew**; a woman says *mislila sem*. The second is an imperative. Both are installed fully in units 12 and 19; for now, learn them as chunks.

grammars.title: Dnevi v tednu — the seven days and where they come from
body: The last column is the one you'll use most. Notice that three days are feminine, and only those three change form.
after: To say "every Monday", use *ob* with the plural: *ob ponedeljkih*, *ob sredah*, *ob petkih*. This is the form you'll see on course timetables and shop opening hours.
*Teden* means week as a stretch of time (seven days), while *nedelja* means Sunday. Don't mix them up: *naslednji teden* = next week, *naslednja nedelja* = next Sunday.

grammars.title: Meseci in datumi — months and dates
body: Slovenian month names are almost the same as English ones, because both borrowed from the same Latin source. All you need to learn is their form when used in a date.
after: In writing, Slovenian dates use **points**, not slashes: **15. 3. 2026**. The order is day-month-year, as in British English — never the American month-first order.

To ask the date: *Kateri datum je danes?* (what's the date today?). The answer uses the ordinary form: *Danes je petnajsti marec.* But as soon as you say something **happens on** that date, the form changes: *Izpit je petnajstega marca.*

grammars.title: Vrstilni števniki — ordinal numbers
body: Ordinals are used for dates, floors, queue numbers, and any kind of order. They behave like adjectives, so they follow the gender and number of their noun.
after: The pattern: add **-i** to the ordinary number. The only irregular ones are the first four — *prvi*, *drugi*, *tretji*, *četrti* — and that's natural; the first numbers are always the oldest in any language (think *first, second* in English).

Because they're adjectives, the ending follows the noun: *prvi dan* (the first day), *prva knjiga* (the first book), *prvo nadstropje* (the first floor). In compounds, only the last number changes: *enaindvajseti* (twenty-first).

sections.title: Letni časi in prazniki — seasons and holidays

blocks.text: Slovenia has four genuinely distinct seasons, and people talk about them every day. Notice that the seasons use *spomladi*, *poleti*, *jeseni*, *pozimi* as adverbs — with no preposition.
Look at **jesen**: it ends in a consonant but is **feminine** — one of the exceptions listed in unit 4. *Dolga jesen*, not *dolg jesen*.

**Prešernov dan** on February 8 deserves a closer look: Slovenia is one of the few countries in the world to make the death day of a **poet** a national holiday. France Prešeren wrote the poem whose stanza is now the national anthem — and the stanza chosen isn't about war or glory, but about the hope that all nations might live in peace. If you want one sentence that instantly warms a Slovenian to you, mention that you know who Prešeren was.
The following sentences use days, dates, and times together — exactly what you need to set up a schedule with a Slovenian.

head: Slovenščina
Say it
English
rows: I have an exam on Monday.
On Wednesday I'm going to Maribor.

blocks.text: Notice that **čez** is used for time ahead (*čez tri dni* = in three days) and **pred** for time behind (*pred tremi dnevi* = three days ago). The same two prepositions are used for space too — *čez most* (across the bridge), *pred pošto* (in front of the post office) — and Slovenian sees no need to keep them apart.

blocks.title: The rhythm of the week in Slovenia
items: Offices and schools start **very early**: many offices open at 7:00, and the first lecture is often just after seven. In return, the afternoon starts at three.
Large stores close on Sundays, and some small shops close early on Saturdays. Plan your shopping for Saturday morning.
A long weekend in Slovenia means people vanish into the mountains or to the Adriatic coast. If you want to invite someone for Saturday, ask early.
